title: The Placenta Is More Powerful—and More Mysterious—Than You Think - Nautilus
gist: Susana Carmona contrasts the placenta's historic spiritual significance, such as Hmong burial rituals, with its modern treatment as biological waste, noting it is increasingly studied in labs as an endocrine and immune interface between mother and child.

insights.claim: Most contemporary societies incinerate the placenta as biological waste after birth, but it is increasingly being studied in laboratories to understand its role as an endocrine and immune interface between mother and child.
insights.speaker: Susana Carmona
insights.so_what: Discarded tissue becoming research material points to growing interest in maternal-fetal biology and related biomedical work.
insights.quote: But increasingly, the organ is ending up on the lab table, where it can teach us how it functions as an endocrine and immune interface between mother and child.

insights.claim: Ancient civilizations treated the placenta as sacred, symbolizing the protective mother-child bond, and burial or cremation rituals persist in some cultures today.
insights.speaker: Susana Carmona
insights.so_what: Cultural attitudes shape how biological material is handled and who consents to its research use.

insights.claim: Members of the Southeast Asian Hmong community bury the placenta at home, believing the soul returns to its birthplace after death to reunite with the placenta before traveling to the spirit world.
insights.speaker: Susana Carmona
insights.so_what: Illustrates enduring cultural practices around birth tissue.

insights.claim: The word placenta means cake in Latin, derived from the Greek plakoenta (flat cake), and a Greco-Roman recipe dated to 160 B.C. describes a flat dessert called placenta made with dough, cheese, honey and bay leaves.
insights.speaker: Susana Carmona
insights.so_what: Etymological background with little direct investment relevance.
